lesson.title: Chemical Personality: How Functional Groups Give Molecules Their Behavior
lesson.summary: Functional groups are small, specific clusters of atoms attached to a carbon skeleton that determine how an organic molecule behaves chemically, from its polarity to its ability to react with other molecules.
lesson.body:
A bare carbon skeleton, as just described, is chemically fairly unreactive on its own. What actually determines how an organic molecule behaves, whether it dissolves in water, whether it acts as an acid or a base, whether it can link up with other molecules, comes down to small, specific clusters of atoms attached to that skeleton called functional groups. The carbon backbone is the scaffold; functional groups are what give a molecule its chemical personality.

A handful of functional groups show up again and again in biological molecules. The hydroxyl group, written -OH, consists of an oxygen bonded to a hydrogen, and because oxygen is highly electronegative, this group is polar and can hydrogen bond with water directly, the same hydrogen bonding covered in water polarity earlier; it is found in sugars and in molecules called alcohols. The carboxyl group, written -COOH, contains a carbon double bonded to one oxygen and single bonded to a hydroxyl, and it is weakly acidic, meaning it can donate the hydrogen from that hydroxyl as a free H+, exactly the acid behavior described in acid-base chemistry; it appears on amino acids and fatty acids. The amino group, written -NH2, is weakly basic and can accept an extra H+ to become positively charged; it too appears on amino acids. The phosphate group carries a negative charge and is central to nucleotides, DNA and RNA backbones, and energy-carrying molecules like ATP. The carbonyl group, a carbon double bonded to oxygen, shows up in sugars in two related forms, an aldehyde when it sits at the end of a carbon chain and a ketone when it sits in the middle.

Swapping which functional group sits on an otherwise identical carbon skeleton can completely change a molecule's identity. Ethanol, the alcohol in fermented beverages, is a two-carbon chain with a hydroxyl group attached; acetic acid, the acid in vinegar, is also a two-carbon molecule but carries a carboxyl group instead. Both are small organic molecules with nearly the same number of carbon and hydrogen atoms, yet one behaves as a mild solvent and the other behaves as a weak acid, purely because of which functional group is attached.

Amino acids show why this matters so much in biology: every amino acid has both an amino group and a carboxyl group attached to a central carbon, along with a variable side chain. The amino group can act as a base and the carboxyl group can act as an acid, so a single amino acid's behavior in water depends on the surrounding pH, tying directly back to the pH scale and buffers covered earlier. Just as importantly, having both a reactive amino group and a reactive carboxyl group on the same molecule is what allows one amino acid to chemically link to the next, since these functional groups are the reactive connection points that participate in bond formation.

This idea, that functional groups act as reactive connection points, extends across all of biochemistry. Sugars link to each other through their hydroxyl groups, fatty acids attach to glycerol through their carboxyl groups, and nucleotides link through their phosphate groups. In every case, it is the functional group, not the carbon skeleton itself, that does the chemical work of joining small building blocks into the large repeating chains known as polymers, which is exactly where the discussion goes next.
